records.title: A small sandwich, still warm
records.alt: A hand lifts a piece of cachorrinho with melted cheese from a plate at Gazela in Porto.
records.photographer: Cervejaria Gazela. Individual photographer not named
records.depiction: Gazela's own historical serving photograph. Plates, fillings and service can change. The drink shown is optional and is not included in this guide.
records.rationale: The actual sandwich and a hand taking a piece make the eating experience concrete. The dark website background, staff group, fries and francesinha photographs were rejected as misleading or weaker subjects.
records.processing: Resized without enlargement and JPEG encoded quality 92. No generative editing.

records.title: The pastry meets the glass
records.alt: A glass of horchata and a sugar-dusted farton sit on a plate with a Daniel-branded napkin.
records.depiction: Horchata and a farton photographed at Daniel. This is historical food context, not a promise of today's glassware, pastry size or branch setting.
records.rationale: The licensed photograph shows both parts of the proposed tasting and identifies Daniel on the napkin. A portrait-format drink-only image was less informative for the visitor.

records.title: A face made with a brush
records.alt: Hand-painted marzipan animal figures, including a pink and white dog, in Kalev's confectionery photograph.
records.photographer: Kalev / Orkla Eesti AS. Individual photographer not named
records.depiction: Kalev's own marzipan photograph illustrates the confectionery medium, not a guaranteed class template or a participant's result. The separate Visit Estonia workshop photographs were excluded after its reuse conditions were reviewed.
records.rationale: The operator's sharp close-up communicates the small edible painting surface directly. It is honestly labelled as finished marzipan, not a documentary image of a session at Rotermann.
records.processing: Resized without enlargement and JPEG encoded quality 92. No generative editing.

records.title: Colour held by a boundary
records.alt: A hand applies green ceramic colour inside a geometric cuerda seca design in a BarroAzul workshop image.
records.photographer: BarroAzul Gestión Cultural. Individual photographer not named
records.depiction: BarroAzul's photograph of cuerda seca work on a larger patterned piece. It illustrates the technique, not the size or design guaranteed in the shorter visitor session.
records.rationale: A close view of colour being applied shows the precise process described in the guide. The older black-and-white workshop image was rejected because it concealed the colour work.
records.processing: Resized without enlargement and JPEG encoded quality 92. No generative editing.

records.title: A pattern carried by a cord
records.alt: Five differently patterned kumihimo cords and small braided accessories arranged against a plain background.
records.depiction: Five kumihimo braid examples photographed by Ködermaus. Technique context only, not Adachi's premises, supplied materials, class patterns or visitor results. The operator's insecure site and separately restricted tourism and DOMYO photographs were not used for media.
records.rationale: The high-resolution licensed comparison makes the resulting braid structures visible without mislabelling another workshop as Adachi. The caption explicitly distinguishes craft context from a venue photograph.
records.processing: Resized without enlargement and JPEG encoded quality 92. No generative editing.

records.rationale: This clear licensed image identifies the actual red vehicle and steep boarding setting. Reflections and obstructed cab views in the other candidates obscured the experience.

records.title: The harbour is a route
records.alt: A red and white HADAG passenger ferry passes close to a Hamburg harbour pier beneath a cloudy sky.

records.rationale: The ferry and public pier make the transport setting legible in a wide crop. A narrow deck portrait and a darker vessel frame were less useful for understanding the crossing.

ImageDescription.value: The building was first built in 1860 and housed public baths, which were intended to stop people from bathing in the Yarra River. The baths were rebuilt in 1903 and designed by John James Clark. Now, it houses a swimming pool, squash courts and a gymnasium.
